metadata.note: Wenatchee's railroad: the Great Northern's Pacific Extension across the Cascades, which had NO coverage on this map -- nothing anywhere near Wenatchee, Leavenworth or Stevens Pass. This is James J. Hill's transcontinental main line and the reason Wenatchee exists in its present form: the Wenatchee Development Company platted the townsite in early 1892 in close consultation with the GN, filing the plat on May 6 1892; the railroad arrived October 17 1892; twice-weekly service was extended to Wenatchee on November 14 1892. For a few months Wenatchee was the end of track while crews fought over Stevens Pass. The last spike of the Pacific Extension was driven in an impromptu ceremony on January 6 1893, one and three-quarter miles east of Scenic -- and Wenatchee incorporated as a city the very next day, January 7 1893. The first crossing used eight switchbacks over the 4,016-ft pass, 13 miles of track to advance 3 miles. The 2.63-mile first Cascade Tunnel (built 1897-1900) replaced them, but the line still ran high and exposed through Wellington, where on the night of March 1 1910 an avalanche triggered by lightning swept two trains into the canyon and killed 96 people -- the worst avalanche disaster in United States history. GN answered with snowsheds over the nine miles between Scenic and Tye (Wellington, renamed after the disaster) by 1913, and ultimately with the 7.8-mile new Cascade Tunnel, begun January 1926 from Scenic, Berne and Mill Creek, dedicated January 12 1929 and still the longest railroad tunnel in the United States. The old alignment over the top was abandoned in 1935 and is now the Iron Goat Trail; it is drawn here as its own feature. NOTE: the existing great_northern.geojson in this repo draws the GN's Chicago-Seattle flagship trains down the modern Amtrak PORTLAND section via Pasco, so its 'Chicago - Seattle' geometry never reaches Seattle, Everett, Stevens Pass or Wenatchee at all -- see 'known_issue_elsewhere'.

https://www.historylink.org/File/9195 (Wenatchee incorporated as a fourth-class city January 7 1893)

https://www.historylink.org/file/10705 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Tunnel (on January 6 1893, in an impromptu ceremony one and three-fourths miles east of Scenic, a plain iron spike completed the Great Northern's Pacific Extension; eight switchbacks laid over Stevens Pass, elevation 4,016 ft, in 1892, requiring 13 miles of track to move 3 miles; the original 2.63-mile Cascade Tunnel built 1897-1900 to eliminate the switchbacks, opened 1900; the new 7.8-mile / 12.6 km tunnel begun January 1926 at Scenic, Berne and Mill Creek, completed January 1929, dedicated January 12 1929; GN abandoned the original alignment in 1935)

metadata.known_issue_elsewhere: great_northern.geojson labels its two features 'Oriental Limited: Chicago - Seattle' and 'Empire Builder: Chicago - Seattle', but their geometry ends at Portland (0.0 km) and comes no closer than 213 km to Seattle, 253 km to Everett, 199 km to Stevens Pass and 131 km to Wenatchee, while passing 1.5 km from Pasco. Its own metadata says the geometry was taken from the modern Amtrak alignment; the modern Empire Builder splits at Spokane into a Seattle section and a Portland section, and the Portland section appears to have been used for both features. The GN flagships ran to Seattle via Wenatchee and Stevens Pass -- this file's corridor. That file has NOT been modified here.
geometry_sources: Main line real-traced from OpenStreetMap (Overpass), shortest rail path routed leg by leg Spokane - Ephrata - Wenatchee - Leavenworth - Berne - Scenic - Skykomish - Everett over the BNSF Scenic and Columbia River subdivisions, yard/siding/spur track penalised. 294.99 mi with NO bridged gaps. Simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 20 m (station points forced as keeps), 3,895 -> 626 points.

Old Cascade crossing real-traced from OSM abandoned railway (the Iron Goat Trail, Horseshoe Tunnel and Old Cascade Tunnel ways), longest path through that abandoned network: 8.92 mi, passing within 0.16 km of Wellington. That length sits close to the documented 'nine miles between Scenic and Tye' that GN snowshedded by 1913, which is good corroboration that this is the right grade.

IMPORTANT LIMIT: the eight 1892 switchbacks themselves are NOT in this geometry -- nothing of them survives in OSM. The old-grade feature is essentially the post-1900 alignment to the first Cascade Tunnel, so its 1893-1900 segment is drawn on a line that is close to, but not identical with, what trains actually ran over in those years. Berne was the weakest station match on the main line at 5.05 km off; all others matched within 1.8 km.

IMPORTANT LIMIT 2: the main-line feature uses ONE geometry -- the modern, post-1929 Cascade Tunnel alignment -- for all three of its eras, so at years before 1929 it draws trains through a tunnel that did not yet exist. The pre-1929 crossing over the top is supplied separately by the gn-old-cascade-crossing feature, which is why both appear together on the map for 1893-1929. Reading them as a pair gives the right picture; reading the blue main line alone for those years does not.
The Everett end meets gn_seattle_bellingham_vancouver.geojson, so Spokane-Wenatchee-Everett-Seattle is now continuous on the map.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: All frequencies and speeds here are estimates, not timetables -- including the deliberately slow figure used for the switchback era. Also unsourced: the exact date GN through passenger service began over the pass (the January 6 1893 last spike is the completion date, not necessarily a first-revenue-train date); the precise 1892 switchback alignment; where exactly the 1892 railhead stood at Wenatchee; Empire Builder Seattle-section timings; and the date BN/BNSF subdivision boundaries took their present form. The Wenatchee-Oroville and Wenatchee-Pasco branches, and the Chelan/Columbia River lines, are not drawn.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: The Great Northern reached Wenatchee on October 17 1892 and extended twice-weekly service there on November 14 1892 -- hence the very long nominal headway. The townsite had been platted earlier that year by the Wenatchee Development Company in consultation with the railroad. For these few months Wenatchee was the end of track while crews worked the switchbacks over Stevens Pass.
